Topic: What guarantees that the sovereign, having been granted absolute power to escape the state of war, does not simply become the greatest threat to those who created him?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
The sovereign is not a solution to the state of war — he is that war, concentrated into a single will and given a throne. Men flee anarchy expecting shelter, and mistake the size of the shelter for its safety, never grasping that the same absolute power which pins their rivals also pins them.

There is no guarantee, and any prince who tells you otherwise is either a fool or preparing to rob you. What restrains him is not oath, not conscience, not the paper covenant he signed — it is fear of his own ruin, the standing armies of neighboring princes, the fickle love of a people who can still be roused to knives if he strips them of property and honor too openly. Security lies not in his goodness but in the narrow corridor between his appetite and his vulnerability.

Absolute power granted without teeth to withdraw it is not government but captivity with better manners.

*He who arms a lion against wolves has only chosen which beast eats him last.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement: Hobbes would have us believe that men, fleeing the terror of nature, must purchase peace by handing one man—or one assembly—a sword no law may ever again turn against him. I call this no compact at all, but a swindle dressed in Latin. A covenant made only between the many and the many binds; a covenant that creates the sovereign as a party outside it binds no one, for he who is judge in his own cause has never left the state of war—he has merely been declared its winner. Government is not the parent of society but its servant, instituted for the convenience of the governed and answerable to a constitution that exists before it and above it, not one that flows from its pleasure. There is no guarantee, none, in Hobbes's scheme; the absolute sovereign is simply the state of war relocated into a single throne, and every tyranny in history is the proof. *Man did not pass through the wilderness to arrive at a master; he who fears the sovereign more than he feared his neighbor has been robbed, not rescued.*
Keynes — Judgement:
The question assumes power is a fixed quantity handed over once and for all; I have never believed in fixed quantities where confidence is concerned.

No contract guarantees anything — Hobbes offers logic, not economics, and logic cannot bind a sovereign who controls the currency, the budget, and the terms of employment. What actually restrains him is that his authority rests on the confidence of those he rules: on stable expectations, functioning markets, employment sustained rather than starved. A sovereign who governs by animal spirits alone, indifferent to the material welfare of his subjects, forfeits the very stability that justified his creation. The Leviathan is never bound by the parchment that made him; he is bound, if at all, by his dependence on the prosperity and confidence of the society he presides over.

There is no guarantee — only the perpetual, practical work of managing confidence, employment, and expectation so that tyranny becomes economically self-defeating.

*The sovereign who starves his subjects' confidence starves his own authority.*
Hayek — Judgement:
The question presumes that binding the sovereign is a design problem to be solved by better contract drafting. It is not.

What Hobbes offers is not order but a single concentrated will substituted for the chaos of many wills — and that is precisely the danger. Knowledge of how to secure peace and prosperity is never held by one mind or one council; it is dispersed among millions, discovered only through the decentralised interplay of individuals following their own purposes under known, general rules. A sovereign powerful enough to abolish the state of war is also powerful enough to abolish the very process by which social order actually generates itself — and history offers no case of such power resisting that temptation indefinitely. There is no guarantee, because the premise that unlimited power can be safely granted in exchange for security is itself the fatal error.

The Leviathan does not end the state of war; it merely gives it a single, permanent, unopposed author.

*The road to a peaceful sovereign and the road to serfdom are, past a certain point of concentrated power, the very same road.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Hobbes asks us to trade the war of all against all for the peace of one man's absolute will — but I have watched too many households run on exactly that bargain to trust it.

Nothing in Hobbes's contract restrains the sovereign but the sovereign's own reason, and I have seen what unaccountable power does to reason: it does not perfect it, it corrupts it, the same way arbitrary authority over women or servants breeds not wisdom in the master but vanity, caprice, and contempt for those beneath him. A power answerable to no one has no incentive to remain just, only to remain powerful. Security bought by surrendering all right of resistance is not security — it is submission dressed as safety, and submission always decays into tyranny, whether in the family or the state.

There is no guarantee, because the whole design removes the very thing — reciprocal right, held and defended by the governed — that could compel one.

*A sovereign who need answer to no one will, in time, answer for nothing.*
